# Executive Summary

<!--
This section provides a condensed view of the entire proposal, one page long.
It should be a comprehensive high-level overview that captures the essence of the proposal, including its goals, methods, expected outcomes, deliverables, and budget.
-->

When a procedure runs over many cases (files, regions, subjects,
parameter sets) and one case fails, the R user needs to see which case
failed and why, re-run that case only, and keep the record of the
original run. When an input file changes, the user needs to know which
cases depend on it. `genproc`, on CRAN since May 2026, gives this with
one call. The user supplies a function and a *mask*, a `data.frame`
with one row per case. `genproc()` runs the function on every row and
returns one object: a log with one row per case and the real traceback
of each failure; a reproducibility snapshot (R and package versions,
the exact mask, a size-and-date fingerprint of every input file named
in the mask); and helpers that compare two runs and re-run only the
cases that failed or whose inputs changed. Parallel execution (on
`future`), non-blocking execution and progress reporting (on
`progressr`) are optional layers that compose on top.

```r
r <- genproc(convert, mask, parallel = parallel_spec(workers = 4))
errors(r)                    # the failed cases, with their tracebacks
diff_inputs(r_previous, r)   # which input files changed since the last run
rerun_failed(r, convert)     # re-run the failed cases only
```

Version 0.2.0 ships these five layers with 13 exported functions, close
to 300 test blocks, continuous integration on Linux, macOS and Windows,
and a documentation site. Its result object follows one compatibility
rule: fields are added, never removed or renamed.

The ambition goes beyond one package: a written, versioned contract for
iterated runs in R (mask, result, errors, retries, reproducibility,
monitoring), published for review and proposed to other package
authors, with `genproc` as its reference implementation. Henrik
Bengtsson, author of `future` and the R Foundation's representative on
the ISC, commented in detail on the outline in April 2026 and saw the
same need; his advice shaped the plan below.

The grant funds twelve months of work, January to December 2027, in
five milestones. Each funded milestone leaves a documented, tested and
usable improvement: (1) the written contract, including the
error-tolerance and retry rules; (2) a backwards-compatible
`genproc_mask` class that implements it; (3) error replay, content-hash
input fingerprints, live monitoring of non-blocking runs and
cancellation; (4) evaluation by outside users and a worked `targets`
integration; (5) a 1.0.0 release with a stable lifecycle and a
succession process.

**Budget: 13 000 USD**, all labour, itemised by milestone. If the ISC
funds only the first three milestones, the community still gets the
contract and a package that is strictly more capable than today.
